en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Ten Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Four Gates.
10. The Kukkuta Jātaka:
“We do not associate with one who has committed evil, nor do we associate with a speaker of falsehood.”
We do not place our trust in one who is wise only for his own sake, nor do we place our trust even in one who speaks excessively.
There are indeed some men who...
Having the nature of a thirsty cow,
they seem to devour their friends with words but not with deeds.
One who is grasped by empty hands,
wrapped in mere words—
a mere scrap of humanity— should not rise up.
In whom there is no gratitude—
for neither women nor men whose minds are ever-changing toward one another— there is none.
Because of their various differences, we do not seek association even with such people;
they have entered upon ignoble deeds.
Now, we do not even trust such a person,
who slays everyone, though he be concealed like a sharpened blade.
Some here, under the guise of friends,
with insincere kindness,
approach [others] by various means.
And we do not hope for even such things as food or wealth where such a person might see them.
The fool creates distrust, and having done so,
he departs after slaying that [trust].
Many, in the guise of friends, [act thus]...
Beings serve those who conceal their faults;
these are like base men, just as a cock serves a falcon.
But he who does not quickly awaken to a matter that has arisen falls under the power of his enemies.
And later he regrets it.
But he who quickly understands a matter that has arisen—
He is released from the oppression of enemies,
like a cock from its cage;
such a one is like a snare cast away in the forest.
A wise person should avoid from afar one who is unrighteous and constantly destructive,
just as a cock avoids a forest of bamboo."
The Kukkuta Jātaka, the tenth.
